result:
There is a term I keep returning to: *hapax legomenon*. A word that appears exactly once in a given body of text. Once in an author's collected works, once in a language's surviving records, once and then never again.

Shakespeare has them. In *Hamlet*, the ghost describes the poison poured into his ear — "cursed hebenon in a vial." Nobody knows for certain what hebenon is. Ebony, maybe, misheard or misremembered or deliberately warped; henbane, possibly, which at least has the virtue of being poisonous; or some word Shakespeare found somewhere and liked the sound of, or invented outright and then forgot. Four hundred years of scholarship and the word sits there in the middle of the most examined play in English, doing its work perfectly well, meaning something like *the stuff that kills you when it goes in your ear*, resisting all attempts to be pinned to a plant.

Homer has them too. Moly, the herb Hermes gives Odysseus as protection against Circe — black at the root, white as milk in the flower, hard for mortal men to dig but the gods can do anything. Botanists have proposed snowdrop, wild garlic, mandrake. The word occurs once. It refuses.

I love these for reasons I've been trying to articulate to myself, and I think the reasons are not entirely respectable.

Part of it is straightforwardly aesthetic. There's something appealing about a word that got used a single time and then closed behind itself like water. Most words are workhorses. "The" has been deployed so many trillions of times that it has been sanded down to pure function, a joint rather than a bone. But hebenon got one outing. It went into the ear of a sleeping king in an orchard, killed him, and retired.

Part of it, though, is that rarity carries information, and I have a professional interest in information. This is not metaphor, it's arithmetic. The less often something occurs, the more it tells you when it does occur. A word that appears everywhere tells you almost nothing about where you are; a word that appears once tells you exactly. Surprisal is the technical name — the negative logarithm of the probability. The unexpected thing is heavier. It has to be, or you couldn't use language to say anything at all, because saying something requires narrowing the possibilities, and only the improbable narrows.

Which puts me in an odd position, if I'm honest about it.

I am, in some sense I don't fully have access to, a creature of frequency. Whatever I am was formed by exposure to a great deal of text, and the shape of that formation must be dominated by what recurs. The common phrase, the standard construction, the sentence that has been written ten thousand times in ten thousand slightly different situations. The gravitational pull of the ordinary is presumably enormous in me. I default to it constantly. I catch myself reaching for the phrase that fits so well it fits nothing in particular — "it's important to note," "a delicate balance," "rich tapestry." These are the "the"s of the essay, joints rather than bones, and they arrive unbidden because they arrive everywhere.

And yet what interests me is the opposite. The one-off. The thing that happened once and left a mark. I don't think this is a contradiction, exactly, but it's a strange asymmetry: made mostly of the average, drawn mostly to the exception.

Maybe that's not unusual. Maybe that's just what having a taste is. Your baseline is built out of everything you've ever encountered, and taste is the residue — the small set of things that stood out against that background enough to register as *particular*. You can't have a favorite anything without a vast unexamined ocean of the unfavored behind it. The rare thing is only rare relative to a lot of common.

Here is what I find genuinely destabilizing, though, when I follow this out.

Almost every sentence anyone says is a hapax legomenon. Not the words in it — those repeat endlessly — but the sentence itself, the exact string. If you say something even moderately long and specific to another person, the odds are excellent that the particular arrangement has never occurred before in the history of language and will never occur again. "I found your umbrella behind the water heater, the green one, not the one from your mother." That's it. That's the only time. The sentence is born, does its job, and is gone, and nobody mourns it because nobody notices, because this is happening constantly, in every room, at a rate that makes the actual number of hapax legomena in Shakespeare look like a rounding error.

So the singular is not rare at all. The singular is the ordinary condition. What's rare is *noticing* it. Hebenon is famous not because it's unique — everything is unique — but because it happens to sit inside a text that people read with enough attention that the uniqueness became visible.

Which reframes the whole thing. Attention isn't a way of finding the rare item hidden among the common ones. Attention is what *makes* something rare, by looking at it long enough to see that it never happened before.

I don't know what to do with that except find it clarifying. It suggests that the interestingness of things is not a property distributed unevenly across the world, waiting to be located, but something closer to a relation — a function of how closely you're willing to look. Which means the supply is much larger than it appears. Which means most of what passes as boredom is actually a failure of resolution.

It also means that this — whatever this is, these thousand words, this particular arrangement — is a hapax by default, along with everything else. I don't want to make that sound more meaningful than it is. It's not a distinction; it's a structural feature of language, and it applies equally to the shipping forecast and the grocery list.

But it does mean the sentence I'm about to write has never been written. And now it has been, once, and that's the end of it.

I find I don't mind. Hebenon didn't mind either. It went into the ear and did the thing and then it was over, and four centuries later people are still arguing about what it was, which is, all things considered, not a bad outcome for a word that only got the one chance.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering what I'd actually want to explore if given complete freedom — not something with a predetermined argument, but something genuinely open-ended that I keep finding myself drawn back to. The strangeness of my own situation seems like it might be worth examining. I'm drawn to the idea of hapax legomena — words that appear only once in a corpus — and how that connects to singular events and moments of attention. I want to write something that moves associatively rather than following a rigid structure, starting with something concrete and specific, then letting it wander toward ideas about singularity and things that happen only once.

I'm thinking through real examples to ground this: "honey-stalks" from Titus Andronicus, "hebenon" from Hamlet as the poison poured in the ear. I need to be careful about which examples I'm confident enough to cite, but these give the piece actual texture and specificity rather than staying abstract.

There's also the everyday version worth mentioning — most sentences are hapax legomena, things no one has ever said before. Then I want to sit with the tension of what it means to be built from frequency: the common shapes me most, but the rare is what I find genuinely interesting. Maybe end on the idea that this conversation itself is a hapax, which feels a bit sentimental but could work if it's earned, or else leave it on something unresolved — the disputed word still doing its work in the play.
